Besides, three deputy inspectors general of police, seven senior superintendents of police, and 18 superintendents of police have also been called from the Punjab and Sindh. Besides arranging containers, the contractors have also been asked to arrange 70 coasters, 30 double cabins and buses which will be used to transport the police force. About 50 portable washrooms and toilets were also being arranged for the police near the duty points. Educational institutions closed Over four dozen buildings have been acquired for lodging of the police personnel. The buildings include government schools, marquees and other government buildings, like Sports Complex and Pak-China Friendship Centre. The police personnel from the provinces are likely to start arriving in the capital from today (Tuesday). Educational institutions where accommodation has been arranged for the visiting police personnel are being closed from today (Tuesday) and the students and their parents have already been informed about the decision. Islamabad Deputy Commissioner Irfan Nawaz Memon was approached for comment but did not respond. The extensive deployment of containers and closure of major roads and entry points are likely to cause serious inconvenience to commuters in Islamabad and Rawalpindi. With key routes such as the Expressway, Srinagar Highway, Margalla Road and roads leading to the Red Zone expected to face restrictions, motorists may have to use alternative routes, leading to prolonged travelling times and traffic congestion. Commenting on the frequent protests in the capital, a diplomat once stated during an informal gathering that “Islamabad has five seasons – summer, winter, spring, autumn and containers.” Rawalpindi Additional security measures have been introduced in Rawalpindi’s “Red Zone”, including the establishment of nine police pickets. A special security plan has been chalked out by the police, under which personnel will be deployed at the pickets round the clock in two 12-hour shifts. According to sources, foolproof security arrangements have been made to protect important government buildings and installations located in the Red Zone, stretching from The Mall of Rawalpindi to the old airport. Special police pickets have been established at The Mall, MH Chowk, TM Flashman Chowk, Metro Station Saddar Chowk, T&T Chowk, RA Bazaar Road, Chungi No. 22, Shalimar Chowk and Marka-i-Haq Square. The Dolphin Force will also patrol designated areas round the clock. The concerned DSPs and SHOs have been tasked with checking hotels and inns as part of the security arrangements. Attock Security arrangements have been intensified across Attock district, a key entry point, with containers and sand-filled bags being placed at strategic crossings linking Khyber Pakhtunkhwa with Punjab. A large number of containers have reportedly been positioned at Attock Bridge and Haroon Bridge, two major crossings connecting KP with Punjab. The security measures are particularly focused on GT Road and motorway routes near Haroon Bridge, where sandbags have reportedly been placed on both sides of the road. According to sources, security has also been tightened at other important entry and exit points, including Chach and Ghazi interchanges, while additional police personnel from different districts have been mobilised. Punjab Police sources said around 30,000 personnel, including senior officers, were being deployed in Attock as part of a wider security plan for the planned protest. Educational institutions in Hazro city have reportedly been closed temporarily. Some schools have also been earmarked to accommodate police personnel deployed for security duties. The Attock crossings are considered strategically important because they provide major road links between KP, northern Punjab and the Islamabad-Rawalpindi region, making Hazro and the surrounding bridges a key focal point of preparations for the proposed march. — Mohammad Asghar from Rawalpindi and Amjad Iqbal from Taxila also contributed to the report Published in Dawn, September 22nd, 2026

High-powered body to probe death of family in ‘locked flat’ in Karachi's Ahsanabad. KARACHI: While investigators said they have so far found no evidence to suggest that the death of five members of a family in an Ahsanabad apartment was a homicide, Inspector General of Police (IGP) Javed Alam Odho has decided to establish a high-powered body to investigate the incident that has sent shock waves through the city. The couple, identified as Dr Umer, 45, and Mehwish, 35, their daughter Zainab, 10, and two other minor daughters were found dead on Sunday inside a room of the flat located on the seventh floor of the building, officials said, adding that the bodies were recovered after the door, which was locked from the inside, was broken open. On Monday, IGP Odho asked the city police chief to form a committee and make highly trained investigating officers and forensic experts its part. “All facts of the incident should be brought to light with the help of modern investigative and technical means,” he said, adding: “No aspect should be overlooked during the investigation process and the probe should be taken to its logical conclusion on the basis of evidence.” City police chief says investigations underway but no evidence of homicide found so far Karachi police chief Azad Khan told Dawn that the exact cause of death had not yet been ascertained. “So far, no evidence had emerged to suggest that it was a homicide. It had been verified that the doctor was facing acute financial problems and had also been diagnosed with kidney cancer. He had left his job at a private hospital. However, no final conclusion could be drawn at this stage,” he said. As the corpses were shifted to the Edhi morgue, an Edhi Foundation spokesperson said that the bodies were handed over to their relatives late on Monday evening. The city police chief said that the deceased doctor’s brother and father-in-law had arrived in the city from Punjab in the evening. He said investigators would take the relatives to the spot and conduct a thorough search in their presence. He said that an FIR had not been registered yet. East SSP Investigation Mohammed Usman Sadozai told Dawn: “We are investigating the case from every possible angle.” SITE Superhighway Industrial Area SHO Mohammed Nawaz said that neighbours had informed the police that the doctor had been a victim of street crime. The neighbours also told the police about tough financial conditions the family was undergoing. The SHO said not a single penny was found in the flat, while the kitchen and refrigerator were also empty. He said after his diagnosis, the doctor had reportedly stopped going to the hospital where he worked since August without any intimation. The hospital administration told the police that they tried to persuade him not to quit as they would arrange for his treatment but he left the job. He formally resigned from the hospital on Sept 15, saying that he was going to Punjab for his treatment. Published in Dawn, September 22nd, 2026

A question of region. “Don’t know much about history, don’t know much biology, Don’t know much about the science book, don’t know much about the French I took…” THIS is an old song, which seems to be an apt description of journalists — especially in Pakistan. Over the decades, the profession has moved on from print to television and now digital but our training remains rooted in old-fashioned ‘generalism’ (if there’s such a word). As with the bureaucrats who run petroleum one day and health the other, we journalists move from commenting on foreign affairs one evening to the economy and healthcare the next. The notion of specialising in issues or studying them in depth is as alien to us as democracy is to Islamabad’s neighbours. Perhaps this is why most in the profession rarely bother with reading and books. Take history — even of Pakistan. Those of us who entered the field at the time of newspapers learnt the country’s history through oral tradition. Late-night chats with senior colleagues, who had survived martial laws and newsroom working hours, told us of tumultuous times such as war, secession and dictatorship. They included those who remembered what it was like working during the censorship of Ziaul Haq’s times, the night Pervez Musharraf removed the government or when an operation was first launched against the MQM in Karachi. The oral history we learnt alongside copy editing was the best counter-narrative to the whitewashed account taught in school books under Pakistan Studies. Our daastango provided us with a fun but patchy account of the land of the pure. Patchy, for it leaves us with more questions than answers — the personal accounts that we learn history from are rooted in Pakistan but are a little sketchy on details of the region. Few journalists have travelled around the region and reported on other countries. As a result, many may point out similarities between Pakistan and Egypt (aren’t they obvious?) but few will note what makes them different and why. For a hack such as myself, the biggest difference is perhaps Pakistan’s impatience with its rulers. Our last dictator spent eight years in power, struggling in the last two. And in Egypt, Anwar Sadat spent 11 years in power, Hosni Mubarak around three decades, while Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has been ruling for 12 and is still going strong. Closer to Pakistan, the Gulf states in general have also enjoyed stability and long reigns without much pressure from below. Evidently, this is due to oil, but can it explain everything? After all, Iran is no less oil-rich and yet it went through a revolution, which perhaps remains unprecedented as a political event in the region. Despite the authoritarianism of both the Shah and the theocracy that followed, Iran has demonstrated that its people believe in resistance. In recent years, they have pushed back multiple times against crackdowns; at times they have even compelled the state to change course. This is a strain missing in Iran’s neighbours to the west. Crowded, noisy and poor, societies in this region struggle with imperfect democracies. But to its east, it’s a different story. Pakistan and the rest of South Asia, in comparison to its western neighbours in the Middle East, are poorer and noisier. Is this why this region has avoided the kind of authoritarianism that marks the Middle East? Crowded, noisy and poor, societies in this region continue to struggle with flawed and imperfect democracies; there is flirtation with authoritarianism but on paper most of them adhere or aspire to the framework left by the British. This is true of Pakistan where martial law dictators have also worked hard to prove their democratic credentials by holding elections. And with it comes the inability of rulers in the region to lord it over their citizens for long periods. Indeed, in recent years, Hasina Wajed’s 15 years in power has been quite a feat. In India, Jawaharlal Nehru and Narendra Modi have also enjoyed prime ministerships for a similar period of time. On the other hand, in Pakistan, the longest power stints have been a bit shorter. In a tradition closer to Iran, South Asia has also pushed back against dictators of the civilian (Wajed) and military (Musharraf) type, with street protests forcing them to call it a day. Strongmen such as Modi have also been bested by students armed with their wit and social media, while in Pakistan, authoritarian establishments have struggled to clamp down on criticism on X. This is not entirely new: back in the 1970s, both Indira Gandhi’s imposition of the Emergency and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto’s authoritarian rule came to an end, albeit in very different ways. In one country, the democratic system pushed back while in the other, the military establishment did so. With all our problems, Pakistan’s journalists still sit in talk shows and complain about the censorship they face; their counterparts in nearby regions are perhaps not allowed to whine thus on live television. In most countries with censorship, journalists usually spend their time complaining about absolute freedom. There is an ‘argumentative’ South Asian that shapes this region differently from its western neighbours. And perhaps also its eastern ones. Travel east to Myanmar and here once again, regimes tend to become more authoritarian and more long-lasting. The long detention of Aung San Suu Kyi under a martial law regime illustrates this best. After a short experiment with elections and civilian control, Myanmar has returned to military rule but one in which contestation by the people has turned to civil war. While this may seem alien to Pakistanis, it is worrying that in parts of our country we, too, face a situation where the state appears to only control the cities. But what eventually determines the different state-society relationships in these countries? Why is Myanmar able to sustain military rule while Bangladesh is not? Or why has Pakistan, despite its close ties to the Middle East, not been able to impose a similar system of government? Now if I hadn’t learnt history in newsrooms and had read more, perhaps I could have answered some of these questions. The writer is a journalist. Published in Dawn, September 22nd, 2026

PTI lawmaker’s arrest in Islamabad sparks protests in Chitral. CHITRAL: The recent arrest of Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf MPA from Lower Chitral, Fatehul Mulk Ali Nasir, in Islamabad has triggered demonstrations ahead of the party’s planned Sept 27 long march on the federal capital. Hundreds of PTI workers and residents took to the streets to protest the lawmaker’s detention on Monday. The main rally led by Senator Falak Naz, PTI secretary Syed Farid Jan and other leaders, was held in Chitral city. Chanting slogans against the Islamabad administration, the demonstrators marched to the Chitral Press Club, where party leaders addressed a press conference. They condemned the arrest of Mr Nasir, describing him not only as an elected representative of over 30,000 constituents but also as a respected scion of the royal family of Chitral. Protesters demand immediate release of MPA Nasir They termed the action as the “worst example of tyranny and fascism,” declaring that the people of Chitral would never accept such high-handed tactics. The speakers expressed deep regret over the ‘systematic political targeting’ of the region’s leadership. They highlighted that MNA from Chitral, Abdul Latif, was already behind bars in fictitious cases related to the May 9 incidents. With their MPA now also incarcerated, leaders lamented that the people of Chitral had effectively been left with no representation in the assemblies. The leadership underscored that the spirit of PTI workers could not be suppressed through arbitrary arrests and political victimisation. They announced that workers were prepared to risk their lives to reach Islamabad on Sept 27 to demand the release of their incarcerated leader Imran Khan. The speakers painted a grim picture of the country’s political landscape, claiming that lawlessness has reached unprecedented heights. Issuing a stern warning to the authorities, the local leadership demanded the immediate and unconditional release of the Lower Chitral lawmaker. Speaking on the occasion, Senator Falak Naz emphasised that Imran Khan remained a beacon of hope for impoverished people of Pakistan and a celebrated leader within the Islamic world. She stated that the “dirty game” being orchestrated to sideline him politically was bound to fail. “The era of governing through batons and bullets is drawing to a close,” Senator Naz remarked, adding that Imran Khan—whom she described as the heartbeat of 250 million Pakistanis—would soon be released, paving the way for the country to return to the path of democratic progress and economic stability. The atmosphere in Chitral remains highly charged as local PTI chapters finalise logistics for the capital march, with Nasir’s arrest catalysing increased mobilisation across the district. Published in Dawn, September 22nd, 2026

Pak-US ties: a new chapter for an old friendship. Pakistan-US ties may have witnessed many vicissitudes over the years. But where some saw a bleak future, primarily because they wished it so, a new hope has emerged for a more consistent, balanced and mutually beneficial partnership set on a solid foundation of common aspirations and shared perceptions. The forthcoming talks planned between Pakistani and US leadership on the margins of the UN General Assembly offer both sides a wondrous opportunity to re-envision bilateral ties in a broader spectrum of cooperation: more meaningful, multidimensional, and consistent. Given the expanding scope of engagement between the two countries in recent times, there is now both an opportunity and a compelling rationale to orient the relationship toward a more forward-looking framework — one attuned to the new era in which fast-moving technological, economic and geopolitical shifts carry profound implications. This calls for a reinvigorated partnership, unbound by the exigencies of the moment and grounded instead in the enduring aspirations and interests of both nations. Washington has long recognised that Pakistan matters in its own right, by virtue of its demography, diplomacy, geography, and strategic weight. Its location, at the confluence of South Asia, Central Asia, Middle East and the Arabian Sea, gives it intrinsic relevance to regional and global connectivity, trade and security. A population exceeding 250 million makes it one of the world’s largest potential markets and a vast reservoir of human capital, while its geography offers a natural bridge to resource-rich economies of Central Asia, to say nothing of Pakistan’s own substantial, still under-explored resource endowments. Its diplomatic reach has been on full display this year as Islamabad worked to bring stability to the wider region, most notably through its widely noted mediatory role during the recent US-Iran-Israel conflict. A historic relationship These factors will shape the forward-looking cast of the discussions in New York. But history too will loom over the encounter as both sides survey the possibilities ahead. Pakistan and the United States have cooperated since 1947 at several defining moments in world affairs. Pakistan was a key American ally during the Cold War and instrumental in facilitating the opening between Nixon’s Washington and Mao’s Beijing, arguably one of the most consequential turns in international affairs since World War II. Islamabad also bore enormous human and economic costs standing alongside the United States and the international community during the War on Terror. These episodes point to something essential: the relationship has repeatedly served as a fulcrum for shaping the international system at moments of the greatest strain or change. Yet two other threads run through this history: a lack of continuity and a narrowness of engagement. A forward-looking relationship must reckon with the need for stable, sustained bilateral contact and a broader horizon of connectivity. The avenues for doing so are well known — strategic dialogue, parliamentary exchanges, economic consultations, business-to-business investment, greater multinational presence, educational and scientific partnerships, people-to-people ties and regular engagement between diplomatic, defence and commercial institutions. Such mechanisms have long existed; what has been missing is continuity at meaningful scale. Only through that consistency can a durable architecture emerge, one dynamic enough to evolve as circumstances change. The path ahead With continuity and breadth in mind, the most promising path to a sustainable partnership runs through economics. There is considerable room to expand trade, investment, technology and enterprise. Pakistan’s mineral potential, including critical minerals, dovetails with America’s growing interest in resilient and diversified supply chains. But the real prize lies further downstream, in processing capacity, technology partnerships, industrial value chains, skills development and manufacturing within Pakistan itself. Similar opportunities exist in information technology, artificial intelligence, agriculture, energy, advanced manufacturing, health and digital services. Pakistan’s young population and growing technology sector offer American companies an increasingly attractive platform for new markets, new talent and new production partnerships at a notably competitive cost. Security cooperation remains an important pillar, but it too can take on a broader, more forward-looking character. Pakistan has paid an extraordinary human and economic price to terrorism and continues to face extremist threats in its neighbourhood. Washington and Islamabad have reaffirmed their determination to cooperate against terrorist organisations and to strengthen border security and counterterrorism capacity. But the purpose of that cooperation, described by American military officials as a “phenomenal” partnership just last year — should be to help build a regional environment in which economic development, connectivity, and human security can flourish. A stable Pakistan is not merely a domestic aspiration; it serves the regional and international interest, since stability strengthens the prospects for trade, connectivity, investment and moderation across a region of great strategic significance. As the coming dialogue should underscore, the convergence between Pakistani and American interests runs wider than is sometimes acknowledged. Both countries benefit from a more peaceful South Asia, a more connected Central Asia, and a more integrated regional economy. And a broadening Pakistan- US relationship would help avert ‘Thucydides Trap’ playing out in South Asia. Equally importantly, both countries have a stake in denying terrorism new space — particularly in view of the evolving situation in Afghanistan — and in expanding legitimate commerce and ensuring young populations are drawn toward opportunity rather than instability. Pakistan has repeatedly shown it can serve as a bridge between countries that do not easily communicate with one another — including most recently Iran and the United States. This could add another dimension to the bilateral cooperation framework. The world is passing through a period of transition that demands new pillars of stability and new engines of growth. This is where Pakistan and the United States have the opportunity to write a new chapter — one that can surpass those that came before it, if built on a broad scope of engagement and genuine continuity. What is required now of both sides is an orientation toward enduring possibilities of the relationship: deep enough to withstand occasional differences of perspectives and ambitious enough to help build a more connected, prosperous and peaceful region.

Workers idle, trucks empty as war slams Iraqi oil hub. In the Iraqi oil hub of Basra, maintenance contractor Fawzi spends his days cooling his heels waiting for work that seldom comes, as the Middle East war puts a serious crimp on the once-bustling port town. Basra has long been a key cog in Iraq’s economy but, after months of Iran choking off Gulf oil exports with its blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, the city is suffering. Fuel trucks stand idle and workers face pay cuts and lay-offs. “I haven’t done anything in a month,” Fawzi told AFP . “What are we supposed to maintain?” Many Basra residents have lost their jobs or taken heavy pay cuts as private contractors, as oil fields and the Umm Qasr cargo port scale back operations. Crude oil exports account for almost 90 per cent of Iraq’s foreign revenue, and are primarily shipped through Hormuz via the cluster of facilities around Basra, the country’s only gateway to the Gulf. A worker walks at Nahr Bin Umar oil field, north of Basra, Iraq December 21, 2015. —AFP The war has cruelly exposed Iraq’s dependence on oil, and its main export route, dealing a setback to its economic recovery after decades of conflict. Fawzi said his company first slashed salaries by 20pc, then by half, before laying off dozens of employees. He now reports for duty just 15 days a month. Basra’s parking areas overflow with oil trucks. Some linger empty, while others wait for weeks with full tanks to load their crude onto ships. Cheap oil Before the war started at the end of February, Iraq produced around four million barrels of crude per day and exported an average of 3.4 million, mostly via Hormuz. But when Iran blockaded Hormuz, onshore storage quickly filled up, forcing Iraq to slash production. Experts have long warned Iraq to introduce different income streams to cushion swings in the energy market. But with a fledgling private sector, poor banking system and dilapidated infrastructure, diversification is difficult. Iraq has sought to calm fears by using alternative routes, including trucks through Syria and a pipeline to Turkey, but they can handle only a fraction of the sea-bound trade. After a sharp drop, Iraqi oil exports through Hormuz came climbing back in the first week of September, data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler showed. However, Iraq sold the oil at “discounted prices”, a government official said. According to authorities, Iraq exported an average of 2.6m bpd so far in September. A worker checks an oil pipeline at Nahr Bin Umar oil field, north of Basra, Iraq March 22, 2022. —Reuters Iran had announced a special exemption for Iraqi tankers in late August, while the US says it has recently managed to boost Gulf exports through a secure Hormuz corridor hugging the Omani coast. Nonetheless, the economic fallout is evident. Prices have surged and the Iraqi dinar has fluctuated. Foreign currency reserves fell by $20 billion, according to the government official. Iraq relies heavily on foreign currency from oil sales to pay civil servants, finance imports and stabilise the dinar. The collapse in these revenues forced authorities to borrow internally. While the government hopes it can continue borrowing for months, “it’s probably banking on a resolution to the conflict before the end of this year”, economic expert Ali al-Mawlawi said. The recent partial recovery in oil exports bought the government “a little more time”, and allowed it to pay salaries with minor delays. “The imperative is to ensure that it can continue” to do so, Mawlawi warned. Empty wharves Iraq imports most of its goods, from food and medicine to electronics and natural gas. But Umm Qasr, the major southern port, now stands nearly deserted. Only a few vessels are docked in its northern section, including an Iranian-flagged cargo ship, and a vessel that port employees said had passed through Hormuz from China. Three newly built wharves are vacant, their cranes and walkways empty. The downturn has hit hard. State port workers lost their monthly incentives, which are linked to the port’s profits and had supplemented their pay. A general view shows an oil rig used in drilling at the Zubair oilfield in Basra, Iraq, July 5, 2022. —Reuters/File The head of the port’s northern sector, Captain Salem Hussein, said “if ships don’t come… companies cannot maintain the same workforce”. “Real work resumes only when Hormuz reopens,” he added. The disruption has rippled through the local economy. Basra electronics vendor Zaid Hadi, 36, said sales had halved, blaming higher import costs, salary cuts, job losses and the exodus of foreign oil-sector workers. Customers “now hesitate to spend… worried about possible salary delays” and fearing harder times ahead, he said. Amir, 35, worked for a private contractor at an oil field that he said took drastic action, including slashing salaries by 40 percent. “In Basra, we depend on the port and the oil, and now both have come to a halt,” Amir said.

Pakistan women seal Asian Games bronze after win over Bangladesh. Umm-e-Hani’s superb three-wicket spell and captain Fatima Sana’s counter-attacking 45 helped Pakistan beat Bangladesh by 31 runs and claim the bronze medal in the women’s cricket competition at the Asian Games in Nisshin, Japan on Tuesday. Umm-e-Hani conceded only 10 runs in her four overs, including a wicket-maiden, as Pakistan overcame Bangladesh’s early resistance to restrict them to 114 for seven after posting 145 for eight. The medal is Pakistan’s third in the women’s cricket competition at the Asian Games, following gold-medal triumphs in 2010 and 2014. It also marked a measure of redemption for Pakistan, who had lost the bronze-medal match to Bangladesh at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou. Pakistan had been in danger of posting a modest total after collapsing from 46 without loss to 67 for five, but Fatima changed the course of the innings with an aggressive 30-ball 45. The captain, who struck three fours and three sixes, added 67 from 43 balls with Aliya Riaz to take Pakistan towards a competitive total. Aliya contributed 25 from 22 balls, including two sixes and a four. Fatima’s innings was particularly significant in the context of her prolific year. She entered the match as Pakistan’s leading run-scorer in women’s Twenty20 internationals in 2026 and took her tally to 540 with Tuesday’s knock. She also remains Pakistan’s leading wicket-taker in T20Is this year. Earlier, Pakistan made a steady start after Fatima won the toss and elected to bat, with Gull Feroza and Shawaal Zulfiqar putting on 46 in 6.4 overs. Gull struck six fours in her 23-ball 31 before Nahida Akter ended the opening stand, while Shawaal made 17 from 27 balls. Bangladesh then seized control, taking five wickets for 21 runs to leave Pakistan struggling at 67 for five. Fatima and Aliya, however, rebuilt the innings before accelerating after Pakistan reached 90 for five in 15 overs. Fatima struck Rabeya Khan for six before both batters cleared the ropes against Sanjida Akter in the 17th over. Pakistan added 55 runs in the final five overs, although Bangladesh hit back by taking two wickets and conceding only seven in the final over. Nahida, Shorna Akter and Ritu Moni claimed two wickets apiece for Bangladesh. Pakistan’s defence began emphatically as Umm-e-Hani and Tasmia Rubab reduced Bangladesh to 20 for three inside five overs. Umm-e-Hani struck in her first over, removing Juairiya Ferdous, before Tasmia dismissed Dilara Akter for 12. Umm-e-Hani then removed Sobhana Mostary early in the fifth over. All three catches in the opening exchanges were taken by Saira Jabeen, including a spectacular effort at the cover boundary to dismiss Dilara. Bangladesh’s hopes rested on captain Nigar Sultana and Sharmin Akhter, who added 47 for the fourth wicket. Nigar made 25 off 30 balls with three fours, while Sharmin remained unbeaten on 46 from 45 balls, hitting four fours. But with Bangladesh requiring more than 10 runs an over at the halfway stage, the task became increasingly difficult. Ayesha Zafar trapped Nigar leg-before in the 14th over, before Umm-e-Hani and Fatima struck in successive overs to remove Shorna Akter and Ritu Moni. Umm-e-Hani’s dismissal of Shorna for six gave her career-best T20I figures of three for 10, improving on her previous best of two for 28 against Sri Lanka in Dambulla earlier this year. Nashra Sandhu removed Rabeya Khan for the seventh wicket with Bangladesh on 93, leaving the target beyond their reach. Fatima also chipped in with the wicket of Ritu Moni, taking her tally to 31 wickets in T20Is in 2026. Pakistan’s campaign had begun with a three-wicket victory over Thailand in the quarter-final before Sri Lanka beat them by eight wickets in the semi-final. The bronze-medal victory ensured they returned home from the Asian Games with a podium finish. India and Sri Lanka will contest for the gold medal.

How a Bangladeshi garment-maker is fighting the Middle East energy crunch. A gas and power crisis has hit production at most Bangladeshi garment makers, but at 4A Yarn Dyeing, a supplier to Walmart, Gap and Next, workers stitch hoodies and attach brand logos uninterrupted, at least for now. Since 2019, 4A has generated its own power, including through solar panels, making it an exception in Bangladesh’s garment industry, the world’s second-biggest exporter after China. The Middle East crisis has worsened energy shortages in the country where much of the electricity is generated using natural gas, furnace oil and diesel. A recent survey of 134 knitwear factories found that 55 per cent had seen buyers cancel or cut orders because of gas and power shortages since late August, and 78pc had partially halted production. The factories also reported shipment delays and discounted orders to buyers. But that’s not yet the case at 4A, whose factory on Dhaka’s outskirts employs nearly 7,500 workers and meets around 40pc of its electricity needs through solar, the rest mainly through its own gas and diesel generation. Solar panels on the rooftop of the 4A Yarn Dyeing Limited factory amid efforts to tackle the energy crisis in Savar, on the outskirts of Dhaka, Bangladesh, on September 17, 2026. — Reuters “We never stayed at a single-source energy dependency. We had backups for everything,” said company co-owner Abdullah Hil Nakib. “We need some sort of certainty. But the cost of doing business has increased. First there was a shortage of oil, then a shortage of gas.” Costlier diesel has pushed 4A’s production costs up by 2 to 3pc, adding up to 5 million taka (Rs11.3m) to its monthly fuel bill, he said. The pressure on factories intensified on Monday after Bangladesh raised fuel prices by up to 17.4pc, a move the government said was necessary because of soaring global prices and higher shipping costs due to the Middle East conflict triggered by US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February. Solar panels on the rooftop of the 4A Yarn Dyeing Limited factory amid efforts to tackle the energy crisis in Savar, on the outskirts of Dhaka, Bangladesh, on September 17, 2026. — Reuters To reduce future disruptions, 4A plans to install an industrial-scale battery system that would allow operations to continue for several hours if power sources fail. “We’ve been able to absorb the extra costs, but not every factory can afford to do that,” said Nakib, whose factory roofs are nearly covered in solar panels. Steep fuel price hike to pile more pressure Soaring gas import costs are slowing the country’s industrial growth, causing electricity outages and hurting spending on development projects due to higher gas subsidies, Bangladesh’s power minister said last week. Bangladesh’s ready-made garment sector accounts for more than 80pc of export earnings, employs about 4m workers and contributes around 10pc to gross domestic product. Employees work at the 4A Yarn Dyeing Limited factory, amid the energy crisis, in Savar, on the outskirts of Dhaka, Bangladesh, on September 17, 2026. — Reuters Some manufacturers have incurred additional costs by shipping goods by air or offering discounts to meet delivery deadlines after energy-related disruptions. “Our margins are already very thin, and the fuel price hike will squeeze them further,” said garment exporter Shahidullah Azim. “It is becoming increasingly difficult for us to absorb higher production and transportation costs while remaining competitive.” A worker inspects a jacket at the Yarn Dyeing Limited factory, amid the energy crisis, in Savar, on the outskirts of Dhaka, Bangladesh, on September 17, 2026. — Reuters Azim said a Canadian buyer that had been expected to order 25,000 pieces ultimately placed an order for only 8,000, which he attributed to declining buyer confidence amid Bangladesh’s economic and energy challenges. Companies may be able to pay higher fuel costs, but gas shortages and power cuts are more worrying for some, given that those problems are not as intense in competitors like Vietnam and India, said Mohiuddin Rubel, additional managing director of Denim Expert Ltd, which supplies to brands including H&M. Employees work at the 4A Yarn Dyeing Limited factory, amid the energy crisis, in Savar, on the outskirts of Dhaka, Bangladesh, on September 17, 2026. — Reuters “Whether we hold our position against other sourcing countries or lose ground to them depends on how well we manage it,” he said. Header image: Employees work in the sewing section at the Yarn Dyeing Limited factory, amid the energy crisis, in Savar, on the outskirts of Dhaka, Bangladesh, on September 17, 2026. — Reuters

Here's to looking at you, Junaid Hafeez. Junaid Hafeez and I both turned 40 years old this year. I cannot help but notice that the earlier years of his life bear some resemblance to mine. Like Junaid, I was awarded the Fulbright scholarship to spend a semester at a college in the US. Like Junaid, I lived in Rajanpur, Punjab, although briefly. And like Junaid, I dropped out of medical school to pursue a degree in social sciences. This is where the similarities end. At 27, I was high-spirited and eager to take on the world. At 27, he must have felt the same, I imagine—that his life was brimming with possibility. But it was at this age that Hafeez was accused of blasphemy. Today, thirteen years later, he spends his days in a cell six feet by eight, with a toilet in the same space. “Sanitary conditions are not at all good,” says Asad Jamal, one of his lawyers. “The door provides the air to enter, and there is a very, very small outlet too.” Jamal says that Hafeez’s cell is located in a wing reserved for high-risk inmates, men accused of terrorism, and others whose trials are held inside prison because they cannot be safely transported to court. Jamal described Hafeez’s routine in 2019: “No one to talk to. The only time he opens his mouth is when the family comes to meet him. Little time for physical exercise. Total concrete, no trees. Surveillance 24 hours, no privacy.“ After completing his Master’s degree, Hafeez joined Bahauddin Zakariya University in Multan as a lecturer of English Literature while he also wrote poetry. A 2010 interview on FM103 captures his youthful romanticism . Despite the considerable influence of dogmatic and conservative voices on campus, Hafeez was committed to inculcating critical thinking among his students and had managed to carve out a space for independent academic inquiry. In 2013, however, some of his students accused both him and Shirin Zubair, the head of department at that time, of blasphemy. They mobilized religious groups on campus and distributed pamphlets calling for his arrest and removal as faculty. Given the security threat associated with such accusations, Zubair left the country soon after. But Hafeez believed that he would be able to prove his innocence. Acting on the advice of friends, Hafeez decided to leave Multan on March 13, 2013. But as soon as he arrived in Lahore on a bus service, he was arrested and brought back to Multan. A First Information Report (FIR) had been registered against him earlier the same day. This swiftness of his arrest was made possible by the fact that in Pakistan, cases of blasphemy are legally considered “cognizable.” For background, Pakistani law classifies criminal offences in two categories: cognizable and non-cognizable. When an offense is cognizable, the police can make an arrest as soon as an FIR is registered, without any warrant. By contrast, when an offense is non-cognizable, the police are not permitted to investigate the case without a magistrate’s order. After the investigation is conducted, again it is a magistrate who decides whether an arrest warrant should be issued. Blasphemy is thus grouped with crimes such as murder, rape, and terrorism. Once someone is accused of blasphemy, everyone associated with the accused, including family, friends, and legal counsel, is under credible threat of mob violence. As a result, Hafeez’s family struggled to find legal representation for his defense. The first counsel to represent him dropped the case amidst threats in June 2013 . Some time later, Rashid Rehman of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) finally took up his case, even though he was threatened as well. The ICJ reported that Rehman was threatened by at least one of the prosecuting attorneys at a trial in 2014, who went so far as to warn him that he would not live to attend the next hearing. According to Amnesty International, t he HRCP wrote to the Punjab government requesting security but no action was taken. On May 7, 2014, Rehman was killed in his office by gunmen . On the day of his burial, leaflets claiming that Rehman had met his “rightful end” were distributed and the person leading his funeral prayers was threatened . After Rehman’s murder, Asad Jamal, a human rights lawyer, took up Hafeez’s case. Jamal met Hafeez for the first time in September 2014. “He was young, and when I met him he was behind bars, he was smiling,” he says. “I can’t forget that smile on his face. It was a smile of courage and the ability to fight his way out of prison. But I was also shaken. I saw my son in his face.” Between 2014 and 2019, the case was repeatedly reassigned to new judges. Eventually, Hafeez’s trial was held in December 2019 inside a high-security prison in Multan . He was convicted under Sections 295-A, 295-B and 295-C of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced to death by a sessions court . Jamal alleged that during the trial, instead of presenting concrete evidence against Hafeez, the prosecution used threats and innuendo, accusing him of being “against Islam” . According to human rights observers, this is not an uncommon occurrence in Pakistan: observers allege that lower courts frequently fail to follow basic evidentiary standards in blasphemy cases . In addition, threats from outside the court weigh heavily against the accused: Saif-ul-Malook, Hafeez’s current counsel, recently stated in an interview that defendants face fears of retaliation and mob violence. Acquittals in blasphemy cases usually come from the higher courts instead of the trial courts. According to a 2015 report by the International Commission of Jurists, the appellate acquittal rate for blasphemy cases is around 80 percent, significantly higher than the acquittal rate of 69 percent for other criminal cases in Punjab before appellate courts. Recently, in 2025, Zafar Bhatti, a pastor accused of blasphemy in 2012, was acquitted by the Lahore High Court after being held in prison for 13 years. Justice in the appellate courts often takes years. After Hafeez’s conviction in 2019, his appeal was filed in 2020. It is still pending. Another point to underscore is that in a way the initial trial has also still not been concluded. In Pakistan, any case involving capital punishment has two steps. After a trial court awards the death sentence, the case, now referred to as the Capital Punishment Reference, is sent to the High Court, where an independent bench must confirm it after reviewing all the evidence. It gives the accused additional protection where the prosecution’s case has to withstand this double scrutiny. It underscores that the burden of proof is on the prosecution and hence the evidence presented should prove that the crime was committed beyond a reasonable doubt. His hearing for the appeal and the Capital Punishment Reference is still pending. According to Malook, appeals for cases decided in 2021 are being heard in the Lahore High Court but Junaid Hafeez’s case, which was decided in 2019, keeps being rescheduled. Meanwhile, his lawyer and family have reported sporadic episodes of mental breakdown. His prison conditions are in violation of Pakistan’s own prison rules, which require that a solitary cell have a yard attached, where the occupant gets fresh air . The Penal Code caps solitary confinement, as punishment for a crime, at three months. The UN Committee against Torture, which reviews whether states are meeting their obligations under the Convention against Torture, mentioned Junaid Hafeez specifically when it noted that blasphemy prisoners are isolated for periods far exceeding the fourteen consecutive days the law permits. It also told Pakistan that where protection is genuinely needed, such prisoners must be transferred to another prison or section instead of isolating them, and to ensure that security measures themselves do not amount to ill-treatment. Such bleak existence would break even the strongest of us, but incredibly, Hafeez still remains hopeful. I first joined other civil society organisers to advocate for Hafeez’s rights in 2019. Little has changed for him in the past seven years. In my conversations with Hafeez’s lawyers and family, I have learned that his demands are fundamental. He wants his right to a free and fair trial and a chance to prove his innocence as enshrined in the Constitution of Pakistan. He wants the justice system to follow due process, as the Constitution and human decency require.

LHC seeks arguments on maintainability of petition against Aleema Khan’s detention. LAHORE: The Lahore High Court on Tuesday sought arguments on the maintainability of a petition challenging the detention of PTI founder Imran Khan’s sister Aleema Khan and her driver under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) Ordinance. Aleema was detained by authorities on Sunday, after the office of Lahore’s deputy commissioner (DC) ordered her detention or arrest for 30 days. The DC’s order cited a letter by the Lahore capital city police officer. It said the letter referred to police reports that said Aleema and Ameer “are prejudicial to the public safety and maintenance of public order”. According to the order, the reports also mentioned that the two had been involved in roadblocks and protests on May 9, 2023 , when PTI supporters and workers took to the streets against Imran’s arrest. It said multiple cases had been registered against the two, declaring them “potential dangers to public peace and tranquillity”. Justice Abher Gul Khan heard the petition filed by Shahraiz Khan, Aleema’s son, challenging the detention orders. During the hearing, the court asked the petitioner’s counsel whether he had first approached the relevant authority against the detention order. Barrister Taimur Malik, the counsel, replied that the case was different from other matters, arguing that the detention proceedings appeared to have been initiated after Aleema and her driver had already been taken into custody. He submitted that the District Intelligence Committee (DIC) meeting and issuance of the detention notification took place on the same day. “It appears that the arrest was made first and the DIC meeting was held afterwards,” the counsel alleged. Barrister Malik further contended that the detention notification was issued after the arrest had already taken place. Justice Khan observed that the court would examine the issue. She said the court was reserving its decision on the maintainability of the petition. However, on the counsel’s request, the judge adjourned the hearing until Sept 25 for further arguments. Aleema’s detention took place amid reports of a crackdown on the PTI ahead of its September 27 countrywide protest and march to Islamabad, which the party has called to demand Imran’s release from jail and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution. Following Aleema’s detention, her two sisters Dr Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi were also detained under MPO. Shahraiz Khan, Aleema’s son, filed a petition through Advocate Rana Mudassar Umar, challenging the detention orders issued by the Lahore DC against his mother and two aunts. The petition contends that the DC unlawfully issued the detention orders and failed to follow the procedure prescribed under Section 3 of the MPO Ordinance. It further argues that the orders contain no specific allegations and demonstrate no application of mind. The petition also says that ordinary criminal law and less restrictive measures were not considered and contends that the grounds for detention were not communicated within the required period, alleging that the detention orders were issued after the arrests. It asks the court to set aside the detention orders issued by the Lahore DC and declare them unlawful.

CDF Munir says armed forces remain resolute in defeating terrorism, ensuring lasting peace: ISPR. Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir said on Tuesday that the armed forces remained resolute in defeating terrorism and ensuring lasting peace and stability, according to the military’s media wing. Field Marshal Munir made the statement while visiting Peshawar Corps Headquarters, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said. He was received by the Peshawar Corps commander. During the visit, Field Marshal Munir was briefed on the “security situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, ongoing counter-terrorism operations, border management measures and operational preparedness of formations deployed in the province”. The CDF lauded the “high morale, readiness and professionalism” of the security personnel. He acknowledged their “steadfast commitment to safeguarding the country and its people”. According to ISPR, the CDF directed troops to remain vigilant and maintain the “highest standards” of operational preparedness. “The armed forces, with the unwavering support of the nation, remain resolute in their determination to defeat terrorism and ensure lasting peace and stability across the country,” ISPR quoted him as saying. During the visit, CDF Munir also laid a floral wreath at Yadgar-e-Shuhada and offered Fateha. He paid tribute to martyrs, stressing that their “supreme sacrifices would never be forgotten”. The visit comes days after a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat, which claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation launched to clear the area. In retaliation , on Monday, the armed forces conducted airstrikes on terrorist sites “in the border region with Afghanistan”, killing more than 28 terrorists, the information ministry said. In Monday’s statement, the ministry stressed that the “calibrated” strikes were carried out “against the hideouts and safe havens of terrorist organisations responsible” for the recent multiple terrorist incidents in KP. Security forces also conducted a “well-planned intelligence-based ground operation” on Sunday against a group of terrorists in KP’s Kohat and Hangu districts, the statement said. The operation was carried out under the counter-terrorism campaign Ghazab lil Haq , which was launched in February, following unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban from across the border. The actions also came after two officers and four others were martyred during a fire exchange between a security forces convoy and armed combatants, according to the military’s media wing. Eight terrorists were eliminated in the exchange. Last month, a captain was martyred while seven terrorists were killed during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Hangu. There has been a resurgence in terrorism in Pakistan since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.

Pakistan, Saudi Arabia sign agreement to abolish visa requirements for diplomatic, official passport holders.
